newsitem.title: USA: FBI begins global probe of letter bombs.
newsitem.headline: FBI begins global probe of letter bombs.

text.p: The FBI cast a global net on Friday in its investigation of eight letter bombs mailed from Egypt to the United States, and the State Department warned U.S. embassies to review security measures.

State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said the discovery of bombs over the last two days has prompted a warning to all U.S. embassies and consulates to review security, especially package-screening procedures. Burns also advised U.S. citizens abroad to report any "suspicious mail" delivered to them.
The eighth bomb was discovered on Friday morning at a post office outside the federal prison at Leavenworth, Kansas, an FBI spokesman in Kansas City said.
Like the other seven bombs, Friday's discovery was a thick envelope made to look like a Christmas card and bore an Egyptian postmark, FBI special agent Max Geiman said.

The letter bombs appeared to be made with Semtex, a military-grade explosive widely used among international terrorists, the Washington Post reported in Saturday editions, quoting federal law enforcement officials.
Geiman dismissed a report of a ninth bomb, saying an envelope that at first raised suspicions in the Leavenworth prison mail system was not a bomb and "has no known connection to this situation."

Three bombs turned up in the area around Leavenworth and five were found in Washington. The Washington bombs were addressed to the offices of Al-Hayat, a newspaper leased to Saudi Prince Khalid bin Sultan. Four bombs were found at Al-Hayat's offices and the fifth turned up at the city post office.
The case sparked an international investigation by the Federal Bureau of Investigation.

"We are not only conducting the investigation in the United States, but also are reaching out to friendly foreign intelligence sources to see if they have anything that might be of interest," FBI spokeswoman Susan Lloyd said.
Lloyd, based in Washington, said the FBI asked its legal attache in Egypt to travel to the Egyptian city of Alexandria, which was the postmark on some of the bombs.
"At this point it's still early on in the investigation," she said. "We haven't eliminated any possibilities. As far as enumerating who our suspects might be, it's still too early to do that either."

Lloyd dismissed as "purely speculative" reports that the officials were investigating a possible connection between the cards and key figures in the 1993 bombing of the World Trade Centre and the foiled plot to bomb other New York landmarks.

Mohamed Salameh, one of four militant Moslems jailed for life for the 1993 World Trade Centre bombing, is imprisoned at Leavenworth, according to an attorney in the case. Victor Alvarez, convicted with nine others for plotting to blow up United Nations headquarters and other New York targets, was also at Leavenworth, his attorney said.
Three of Alvarez's co-defendants were from around Alexandria in Egypt.

An attorney with knowledge of the prisoners said Alvarez wrote letters from prison to people all over the United States and overseas about his case, including many to the editor of a prison network newsletter.
Lloyd said the FBI was reviewing debris from four devices found on Thursday at Al-Hayat's offices. The devices were "disrupted" safely by the Washington bomb squad.
The devices discovered at the Leavenworth prison were being shipped to the FBI's laboratory in Washington, Lloyd said.
The letter bombs were meant to explode when opened, but all were intercepted before they went off, the FBI said, adding that the devices would have caused "grave harm" if detonated.
The FBI said on Thursday there might be more such bombs in the mail and urged Americans to be alert for the devices.
